pos: n. (childbirth; the act of being delivered)
etymology: Anglo-French delivree, from deliver, Latin de- and liberare, to set free. In Isaiah 26:17 it renders the Hebrew yalad, to bear, bring forth.
biblical_def: Isaiah's song of the strong city includes a confession of failure in the language of labour. “Like as a woman with child, that draweth near the time of her delivery, is in pain, and crieth out in her pangs; so have we been in thy sight, O LORD” (Isaiah 26:17). Webster cites this verse for delivery as childbirth. But Israel's labour came to nothing: “We have been with child, we have been in pain, we have as it were brought forth wind; we have not wrought any deliverance in the earth; neither have the inhabitants of the world fallen” (Isaiah 26:18). All their striving produced wind. Then God speaks, and what man could not deliver He brings forth: “Thy dead men shall live, together with my dead body shall they arise. Awake and sing, ye that dwell in dust: for thy dew is as the dew of herbs, and the earth shall cast out the dead” (Isaiah 26:19). The true delivery is resurrection, and the earth itself will give birth to the dead.

webster_full: DELIVERY, noun 1. The act of delivering.
2. Release; rescue; as from slavery, restraint, oppression or danger.
3. Surrender; a giving up.
4. A giving or passing from one to another; as the delivery of goods, or of a deed.
5. Utterance; pronunciation; or manner of speaking. He has a good delivery I was charmed with his graceful delivery

corruption_paragraphs: The word is plain. Isaiah 26:19 is sometimes read as national revival only; it is one of the clearest Old Testament promises of bodily resurrection, and the dictionary reads it so, alongside Daniel 12:2.
This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that salvation is God's work. Israel's pangs brought forth wind; the LORD brings forth the dead.

pos: v.i. (to bring forth young before the time; to fail)
etymology: From mis-, wrongly, and carry, Old French carier. In Hosea 9:14 miscarrying renders the Hebrew shakal, to be bereaved, to lose offspring.
biblical_def: Hosea's judgment on Ephraim strikes at the very thing Ephraim's name promised, fruitfulness. “As for Ephraim, their glory shall fly away like a bird, from the birth, and from the womb, and from the conception” (Hosea 9:11). The prophet, torn between grief and agreement with God's justice, breaks into a terrible prayer: “Give them, O LORD: what wilt thou give? give them a miscarrying womb and dry breasts” (Hosea 9:14). Better no children than children raised for slaughter by an idolatrous nation. The sentence ends in exile: “My God will cast them away, because they did not hearken unto him: and they shall be wanderers among the nations” (Hosea 9:17). The miscarrying womb is counted a curse, because Scripture counts children a blessing and every child in the womb a life from God.

1. To bring forth young before the proper time; to suffer abortion.

corruption_summary: The language of the womb has been emptied of the child, so that the deliberate ending of unborn life is called healthcare, when Scripture mourns the loss of a child in the womb as bereavement.
corruption_paragraphs: The Hebrew word Hosea uses is shakal, to be bereaved, the same word used of parents who lose children. Scripture never treats the unborn as tissue: John leaped in his mother's womb (Luke 1:44), and David was fearfully and wonderfully made there (Psalm 139:13-14). Modern law and medicine have redefined deliberate abortion as reproductive care. The dictionary names it the taking of innocent human life.

The principle to recover is the sanctity of life from conception, and compassion for parents who suffer the loss of a child in miscarriage. Their grief is grief for a child, and Scripture honours it as such.

pos: adj. (made of flesh; soft, living, not stone)
etymology: From flesh, Old English flaesc, plus -y. In 2 Corinthians 3:3 it renders the Greek sarkinos, made of flesh, as opposed to sarkikos, fleshly, governed by the flesh.
biblical_def: Paul defends his ministry by pointing to the Corinthians themselves. “Forasmuch as ye are manifestly declared to be the epistle of Christ ministered by us, written not with ink, but with the Spirit of the living God; not in tables of stone, but in fleshy tables of the heart” (2 Corinthians 3:3). The contrast is between the stone tablets of Sinai and living hearts, and it fulfils Ezekiel's promise: “A new heart also will I give you, and a new spirit will I put within you: and I will take away the stony heart out of your flesh, and I will give you an heart of flesh” (Ezekiel 36:26). Jeremiah had promised the same: “I will put my law in their inward parts, and write it in their hearts” (Jeremiah 31:33). Fleshy here is a good word: soft, living, responsive. It must not be confused with fleshly, which in Scripture means governed by the sinful flesh. The new covenant does not abolish the law; it writes it on a fleshy heart.

corruption_summary: Fleshy is confused with fleshly, and the new covenant is set against the law, when Paul's point is the law written on a heart God has made alive.
corruption_paragraphs: The two words differ by a letter and by everything else. Fleshy (Greek sarkinos) describes the material, living flesh; fleshly (Greek sarkikos) describes the sinful disposition. Some readers also take 2 Corinthians 3 as Paul setting the Spirit against the law itself, as antinomian teaching does. Ezekiel and Jeremiah show that the new covenant writes God's law on the heart, so that His people walk in His statutes.
The principle to recover is regeneration. God takes away the heart of stone and gives a heart of flesh, and the moral law that once condemned from stone is now written within.

etymology: From enlarge, Old French enlargier, from en- and large, Latin largus, abundant. In Esther 4:14 it renders the Hebrew revach, space, relief, respite.
biblical_def: Mordecai's message to Esther is the most famous verse in her book, and its first promise is enlargement. “For if thou altogether holdest thy peace at this time, then shall there enlargement and deliverance arise to the Jews from another place; but thou and thy father's house shall be destroyed: and who knoweth whether thou art come to the kingdom for such a time as this?” (Esther 4:14). Webster cites the verse for enlargement as release from distress. Mordecai was sure that God would not let His people perish; the only question was whether Esther would be His instrument. She answered: “Go, gather together all the Jews that are present in Shushan, and fast ye for me,” and then, “so will I go in unto the king, which is not according to the law: and if I perish, I perish” (Esther 4:16). The psalmist uses the same picture of room after confinement: “I called upon the LORD in distress: the LORD answered me, and set me in a large place” (Psalm 118:5).

corruption_summary: Esther 4:14 is turned into a motivational slogan about personal destiny, when Mordecai's confidence rests on God's covenant faithfulness to His people.
corruption_paragraphs: For such a time as this has become a stock phrase of self-help and leadership talks, meaning that each person has a moment of destiny to seize. Mordecai's point is the reverse of self-assertion. Deliverance will come regardless, because God keeps His covenant; Esther's privilege is to be used, and her peril is to refuse.
The principle to recover is providence and duty together. God guarantees the enlargement of His people; His servants are called to risk themselves in obedience without knowing the outcome.

etymology: From month, Old English monath, related to mona, moon, plus -ly. In Isaiah 47:13 the monthly prognosticators renders the Hebrew modi'im lechodashim, those who make known by the new moons.
biblical_def: Isaiah taunts Babylon on the eve of its fall, mocking the experts the empire trusted. “Thou art wearied in the multitude of thy counsels. Let now the astrologers, the stargazers, the monthly prognosticators, stand up, and save thee from these things that shall come upon thee” (Isaiah 47:13). The monthly prognosticators issued forecasts at each new moon, the horoscopes of the ancient world. They could not save themselves: “Behold, they shall be as stubble; the fire shall burn them; they shall not deliver themselves from the power of the flame” (Isaiah 47:14). God had forbidden His own people every such practice: “There shall not be found among you any one that maketh his son or his daughter to pass through the fire, or that useth divination, or an observer of times, or an enchanter, or a witch” (Deuteronomy 18:10). The monthly forecast is still printed in the newspaper, and still powerless to deliver anyone from the judgment of God.

corruption_summary: Astrology's monthly forecasts are treated as harmless entertainment, when Scripture classes them with divination as the counsel of a doomed Babylon.
corruption_paragraphs: Horoscopes, zodiac personality types and astrology apps are popular even among professing Christians, who regard them as amusement. Isaiah names the monthly prognosticators among Babylon's false saviours, and Deuteronomy puts observers of times with witches and enchanters. Seeking guidance from the heavens is turning from the God who made them.

The principle to recover is trust in God's providence and word for guidance. The believer does not consult the new moon; he walks by the word, and leaves the future with the God who declares the end from the beginning.

pos: n. (a flowing in; in Job 38:31, the binding power of a star cluster)
etymology: Latin influentia, a flowing in, from in and fluere, to flow. In Job 38:31 sweet influences renders the Hebrew ma'adannoth, usually taken as bands or chains, the binding of the cluster.
biblical_def: The word appears once, in God's challenge to Job: “Canst thou bind the sweet influences of Pleiades, or loose the bands of Orion?” (Job 38:31). In 1611 influence still carried its astrological sense, a power flowing down from the stars upon the earth, and the translators used it for the Pleiades' cluster bound together in the sky. But the question strips the stars of any rule over men. Who binds them? Not Job, and not the stars themselves: God does. Isaiah makes the same point: “Lift up your eyes on high, and behold who hath created these things, that bringeth out their host by number: he calleth them all by names by the greatness of his might” (Isaiah 40:26). And Jeremiah draws the conclusion for God's people: “Learn not the way of the heathen, and be not dismayed at the signs of heaven; for the heathen are dismayed at them” (Jeremiah 10:2). The only influence that rules a believer's life flows from the throne, not the sky.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): IN'FLUENCE, noun [Latin influens, influo, to flow in; in and fluo, to flow.] Literally, a flowing in, into or on, and referring to substances spiritual or too subtil to be visible, like inspiration. Hence the word was formerly followed by into.
webster_full: IN'FLUENCE, noun [Latin influens, influo, to flow in; in and fluo, to flow.] Literally, a flowing in, into or on, and referring to substances spiritual or too subtil to be visible, like inspiration. Hence the word was formerly followed by into. God hath his influence into the very essence of all things.
1. In a general sense, influence denotes power whose operation is invisible and known only by its effects, or a power whose cause and operation are unseen.
2. The power which celestial bodies are supposed to exert on terrestrial; as the influence of the planets on the birth and fortunes of men; an exploded doctrine of astrology.

3. Moral power; power of truth operating on the mind, rational faculties or will, in persuading or dissuading, as the influence of motives, of arguments, or of prayer. We say, arguments had no influence on the jury. The magistrate is not popular; he has no influence with the people;
4. Physical power; power that affects natural bodies by unseen operation; as, the rays of the sun have an influence in whitening cloth, and in giving a green color to vegetables.
scriptures: Canst thou bind the sweet influences of Pleiades, or loose the bands of Orion?

corruption_summary: Influence, once a term of astrology, now describes a trade in personal reach and persuasion; in both forms it locates power somewhere other than in God.
corruption_paragraphs: Webster (1828) already called the influence of the planets on the birth and fortunes of men an exploded doctrine of astrology. The word has since become the vocabulary of social media, where an influencer is one who shapes opinion and buying, and influence is pursued as power. The modern influencer is treated in its own entry.
The principle to recover is the sovereignty of God over the stars and over men. He binds the Pleiades, numbers the host of heaven, and forbids His people to be dismayed at signs in the sky.

pos: proper n. (the eastern cape of Crete)
etymology: Greek Salmone, the promontory at the eastern end of Crete, now Cape Sidero.
biblical_def: Salmone marks the point where Paul's voyage began to go wrong. Westbound from Myra, the ship fought the wind for days: “And when we had sailed slowly many days, and scarce were come over against Cnidus, the wind not suffering us, we sailed under Crete, over against Salmone” (Acts 27:7). Unable to hold their course, they turned south around Crete's eastern cape to shelter in its lee. “And, hardly passing it, came unto a place which is called The fair havens; nigh whereunto was the city of Lasea” (Acts 27:8). Then came the season's warning: “Now when much time was spent, and when sailing was now dangerous, because the fast was now already past, Paul admonished them” (Acts 27:9). The fast was the Day of Atonement, in early autumn, when the Mediterranean was closing to shipping. Salmone was the turn into danger, and Paul's counsel was ignored.

etymology: From resemble, Old French resembler, from re- and sembler, to seem, Latin similare, to make like. In Zechariah 5:6 it renders the Hebrew 'ayin, eye, appearance, aspect.
biblical_def: Zechariah's seventh vision shows sin being carried out of the land. An angel shows him a measuring basket: “And I said, What is it? And he said, This is an ephah that goeth forth. He said moreover, This is their resemblance through all the earth” (Zechariah 5:6). The ephah is what the people look like, their appearance or eye, a picture of what fills the land. The lid is lifted: “And, behold, there was lifted up a talent of lead: and this is a woman that sitteth in the midst of the ephah” (Zechariah 5:7). The angel names her plainly: “And he said, This is wickedness. And he cast it into the midst of the ephah; and he cast the weight of lead upon the mouth thereof” (Zechariah 5:8). Then two winged women carry the basket away to Shinar, the land of Babel. God does not leave wickedness at home among His people; He seals it, removes it and sends it back where it belongs.

pos: adv. (at equal distance; in the same degree)
etymology: From equal, Latin aequalis, from aequus, even, level, plus -ly. In Exodus 36:22 equally distant renders the Hebrew meshullaboth, joined, set in order, fitted together.
biblical_def: The tabernacle was built to a pattern given on the mount, down to the joints of its boards. God had said: “According to all that I shew thee, after the pattern of the tabernacle, and the pattern of all the instruments thereof, even so shall ye make it” (Exodus 25:9). The instruction for the boards was precise: “Two tenons shall there be in one board, set in order one against another: thus shalt thou make for all the boards of the tabernacle” (Exodus 26:17). Bezaleel did exactly what was commanded: “One board had two tenons, equally distant one from another: thus did he make for all the boards of the tabernacle” (Exodus 36:22). Every board was the same, every joint matched, and the whole house stood true. The tabernacle was a copy of heavenly things (Hebrews 8:5), and its makers had no liberty to improve on the pattern.

pos: proper n. (son of Zorobabel in the genealogy of Christ)
etymology: Greek Abioud, from the Hebrew 'abihud, my father is majesty, from 'ab, father, and hod, splendour, majesty.
biblical_def: Abiud is a name in the line of the Messiah after the exile. Matthew traces it through the deportation: “And after they were brought to Babylon, Jechonias begat Salathiel; and Salathiel begat Zorobabel” (Matthew 1:12). Then come names known only from this list: “And Zorobabel begat Abiud; and Abiud begat Eliakim; and Eliakim begat Azor” (Matthew 1:13). The governor who rebuilt the temple was followed by sons who left no deeds in Scripture, and the royal line of David passed into obscurity, carpenters rather than kings. Yet the line held, generation after generation, until the last link: “And Jacob begat Joseph the husband of Mary, of whom was born Jesus, who is called Christ” (Matthew 1:16). Abiud is a reminder that God keeps His promises through unremarkable generations, and that the Son of David came from a family the world had forgotten.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) gives no entry for Abiud; the name is that of an ancestor of Christ, carried into the Authorized Version from the Greek.

corruption_summary: Matthew's genealogy is dismissed as a theological construction, when it records the real descent through which God kept His promise to David.
corruption_paragraphs: Critical scholars point to the differences between Matthew's and Luke's genealogies and to Matthew's arrangement in three sets of fourteen as evidence that the lists are artificial. The traditional Reformed explanation, that Matthew traces Joseph's legal and royal line while Luke traces Mary's natural line, accounts for the differences, and Matthew's grouping is a memory aid, not an invention.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the historical reality of the incarnation. Christ was born of a real family, in a real line, as the Son of David according to the flesh (Romans 1:3).
